intro.title: Making vectors with c()
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Data is rarely one number. It is a week of step counts, a class of test scores, a list of café orders. In R, a row of values like that is a **vector**, and almost everything in R works on vectors.

You make a vector with `c()`, short for "combine". Separate the values with commas:

```
steps <- c(4200, 8100, 6500, 9900, 3000)
steps
days <- c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri")
days
```

R shows a vector on one line: `[1] 4200 8100 6500 9900 3000`. When a vector is too long for one line, R wraps it, and the number in square brackets at the start of each line tells you the position of the first value on that line, such as `[13]`. That's what the `[1]` has meant all along: a single value is just a vector of length 1.

`length()` tells you how many values a vector holds: `length(steps)` is 5.

A vector holds one kind of value: all numbers, all text, or all `TRUE`/`FALSE`. If you mix them, R turns everything into the most flexible kind, usually text: `c(1, "two", 3)` gives `"1" "two" "3"`. A later quest looks at this more closely.

`c()` also joins vectors together, so you can add values to the end (or the start) of one you already have:

```
steps <- c(steps, 7600)   # add Saturday
length(steps)             # 6
```
intro.sandboxCode:
steps <- c(4200, 8100, 6500, 9900, 3000)
steps
length(steps)
days <- c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri")
days

intro.title: Sequences: :, seq and rep
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Typing every value with `c()` gets tiring. R has quick ways to make vectors that follow a pattern.

A colon makes whole numbers counting by one: `1:10` is 1 to 10, and `10:1` counts down. `seq()` gives you more control: where to start, where to stop, and either the step (`by`) or how many values you want (`length.out`):

```
1:5                              # 1 2 3 4 5
seq(0, 100, by = 25)             # 0 25 50 75 100
seq(1, 2, length.out = 5)        # 1.00 1.25 1.50 1.75 2.00
seq(10, 0, by = -5)              # 10 5 0
```

`seq()` stops at the last value that fits: `seq(0, 10, by = 3)` is 0 3 6 9, without going past 10.

`rep()` repeats. `times` repeats the whole vector; `each` repeats every value before moving on:

```
rep(0, times = 4)                # 0 0 0 0
rep(c("a", "b"), times = 3)      # "a" "b" "a" "b" "a" "b"
rep(c("a", "b"), each = 2)       # "a" "a" "b" "b"
```

These are handy for setting up data: table numbers `1:12`, a price list that goes up in steps, or a label for each group of readings. Watch the brackets with `:` and maths. The colon is worked out before `+` and `-`, so `1:3 + 1` is `2 3 4`, while `1:(3 + 1)` is `1 2 3 4`.
intro.sandboxCode:
1:10
10:1
seq(0, 100, by = 25)
seq(1, 2, length.out = 5)
rep(c("a", "b"), each = 2)

intro.title: Maths on whole vectors
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Here is what makes R so good with data: arithmetic works on a whole vector at once. There is no need to go through the values one by one.

```
prices <- c(2.5, 3, 4.25)
prices * 2        # 5.0 6.0 8.5
prices + 0.5      # 3.00 3.50 4.75
```

Every value is multiplied by 2, or has 0.5 added. Functions such as `round()`, `sqrt()` and `abs()` work the same way, on every value:

```
round(c(1.234, 5.678), 1)   # 1.2 5.7
```

Two vectors of the same length are combined value by value: the first with the first, the second with the second, and so on. That's perfect for data where each position is the same thing, such as the same day or the same person:

```
cups   <- c(3, 5, 2)
price  <- c(2.5, 3, 4.25)
cups * price      # 7.5 15.0 8.5: what each order cost
```

If the lengths differ, R **recycles** the shorter vector, starting it again from the beginning. With a single number that is exactly what you want (it is used for every value). With other lengths it is usually a mistake, and R warns when the longer length isn't a multiple of the shorter one.

Comparisons work on whole vectors too, giving one `TRUE` or `FALSE` per value: `c(4, 9, 6) > 5` is `FALSE TRUE TRUE`. The next stages use that to pick out values.

intro.title: Picking items by position
intro.bodyMarkdown:
To get values out of a vector, put their positions in square brackets after its name. Positions in R start at **1**, not 0:

```
days <- c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri")
days[1]          # "Mon"
days[c(1, 3)]    # "Mon" "Wed"
days[2:4]        # "Tue" "Wed" "Thu"
```

Inside the brackets you can use any vector of positions: one number, a `c()` of several, or a sequence like `2:4`. The values come back in the order you ask for them, so `days[c(3, 1)]` is `"Wed" "Mon"`.

A **minus** sign leaves positions out: `days[-1]` is every day except Monday, and `days[-c(1, 5)]` drops the first and the last.

The last value is at position `length(x)`, so `days[length(days)]` is `"Fri"` however long the vector is. Ask for a position past the end and you get `NA`: `days[9]` is `NA`, because there is no ninth day.

You can also change values in place, by assigning to a position:

```
steps <- c(4200, 8100, 6500)
steps[2] <- 8300   # fix Tuesday's count
steps              # 4200 8300 6500
```
intro.sandboxCode:
days <- c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri")
days[1]
days[c(1, 3)]
days[2:4]
days[-1]
days[length(days)]

intro.title: Picking items by condition
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Most of the time you don't know the positions you want. You want "the days over 8000 steps" or "the cheap items". For that, put a **condition** in the square brackets:

```
steps <- c(4200, 8100, 6500, 9900, 3000)
steps > 8000           # FALSE TRUE FALSE TRUE FALSE
steps[steps > 8000]    # 8100 9900
```

The comparison gives one `TRUE` or `FALSE` per value, and the brackets keep the values where it is `TRUE`. Read `steps[steps > 8000]` as "the steps where the steps are over 8000".

The condition can come from another vector of the same length. That's how you pick matching values across vectors, such as the names of the days with lots of steps:

```
days <- c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri")
days[steps > 8000]     # "Tue" "Thu"
```

Combine conditions with `&` and `|`, just as in the first quest: `steps[steps > 4000 & steps < 9000]` keeps the values between the two.

Because `TRUE` counts as 1, `sum()` of a condition **counts** the values that meet it, and `mean()` gives the **share** that meet it:

```
sum(steps > 8000)      # 2 days
mean(steps > 8000)     # 0.4, that is 40% of the days
```

You can also change all the matching values at once: `steps[steps < 0] <- 0` sets any negative count to 0.

steps > 8000
steps[steps > 8000]

intro.title: Summaries: sum, mean, max
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A summary turns a whole vector into a single number that tells you something about it. These are the ones you will use every day:

| Function | Gives | For `c(4, 8, 6, 2)` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sum()` | the total | `20` |
| `mean()` | the average | `5` |
| `median()` | the middle value | `5` |
| `min()`, `max()` | smallest, largest | `2`, `8` |
| `range()` | smallest and largest together | `2 8` |
| `length()` | how many values | `4` |

The **median** is the middle value once the values are sorted; with an even number of values it is halfway between the two in the middle. It is less pulled about by one extreme value than the mean: for incomes or house prices, the median is often the better "typical" value.

```
orders <- c(12, 7, 15, 9, 11, 8, 120)
mean(orders)     # 26: dragged up by one huge order
median(orders)   # 11
```

`cumsum()` gives a **running total**, one value per position: `cumsum(c(4, 8, 6))` is `4 12 18`. That's handy for "how far so far" questions.

Summaries combine with everything else in this quest. The total of the busy days is `sum(steps[steps > 8000])`, and the average change since last week is `mean(this_week - last_week)`.

```
steps <- c(4200, 8100, 6500, 9900, 3000)
cat("Total:", sum(steps), "steps\n")
cat("Average:", mean(steps), "a day\n")
```

mean(x)
median(x)
range(x)
cumsum(x)

intro.title: Sorting: sort, order and rev
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`sort()` gives the values in order, smallest first. Add `decreasing = TRUE` for largest first. Text is sorted alphabetically:

```
scores <- c(71, 64, 88, 92, 57)
sort(scores)                       # 57 64 71 88 92
sort(scores, decreasing = TRUE)    # 92 88 71 64 57
sort(c("pear", "apple", "fig"))    # "apple" "fig" "pear"
```

`rev()` reverses a vector, whatever its order: `rev(c(1, 5, 3))` is `3 5 1`. `head(x, 3)` gives the first 3 values and `tail(x, 3)` the last 3, so the top three scores are `head(sort(scores, decreasing = TRUE), 3)`.

`order()` is the clever one. Instead of the sorted values, it gives the **positions** in sorted order: "the smallest is at position 5, the next at position 2…".

```
order(scores)      # 5 2 1 3 4
```

Why would you want positions? Because you can use them to sort a second vector by the first. This puts the players in score order, from highest to lowest:

```
players <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cy", "Dee", "Eli")
players[order(scores, decreasing = TRUE)]   # "Dee" "Cy" "Ana" "Ben" "Eli"
```

You will use exactly this to sort the rows of a data table in a later quest. `sort()` and `order()` don't change the vector itself; save the result if you want to keep it.
intro.sandboxCode:
scores <- c(71, 64, 88, 92, 57)
sort(scores)
sort(scores, decreasing = TRUE)
order(scores)
players <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cy", "Dee", "Eli")
players[order(scores, decreasing = TRUE)]

intro.title: NA in vectors
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Real vectors have gaps. One `NA` is enough to make a summary unknown, because R won't guess what the missing value was:

```
steps <- c(4200, NA, 6500, 9900, NA)
sum(steps)     # NA
mean(steps)    # NA
```

When you are happy to work with the values you do have, add `na.rm = TRUE` ("remove NAs"). Most summary functions accept it: `sum()`, `mean()`, `median()`, `min()`, `max()` and `range()`.

```
sum(steps, na.rm = TRUE)    # 20600
mean(steps, na.rm = TRUE)   # 6866.667: the average of the 3 known days
```

Be clear about what that means: the mean of the known days, not of the whole week. Always check how much is missing. `is.na()` works on a whole vector, so `sum(is.na(steps))` counts the gaps:

```
is.na(steps)          # FALSE TRUE FALSE FALSE TRUE
sum(is.na(steps))     # 2 missing days
```

To keep only the known values, pick with `!is.na()`: `steps[!is.na(steps)]` is `4200 6500 9900`. And to fill the gaps with a value, assign to them: `steps[is.na(steps)] <- 0`. Only do that when 0 really is right, such as a day the step counter was off and you know there was no walking.

Watch out with conditions: `steps > 5000` gives `NA` for the missing days, and picking with it puts `NA`s in the result. `which()` in the next stage avoids that.
intro.sandboxCode:
steps <- c(4200, NA, 6500, 9900, NA)
sum(steps)
sum(steps, na.rm = TRUE)
mean(steps, na.rm = TRUE)
sum(is.na(steps))
steps[!is.na(steps)]

intro.title: which, any, all and %in%
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A few more tools answer common questions about a vector.

`which()` gives the **positions** where a condition is `TRUE`. It skips `NA`s, which makes it safer for picking than a plain condition:

```
steps <- c(4200, NA, 9900, 6500, 8800)
which(steps > 8000)          # 3 5
steps[which(steps > 8000)]   # 9900 8800, no NA
```

`which.max()` and `which.min()` give the position of the largest and smallest value. Use that position to look up something matching, such as the day it happened:

```
days <- c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri")
days[which.max(steps)]       # "Wed"
```

`any()` asks "is at least one TRUE?" and `all()` asks "are they all TRUE?". They turn a whole vector of answers into one: `any(steps > 9000, na.rm = TRUE)` is `TRUE`.

`%in%` asks, for each value on the left, "is it one of these?". It is much tidier than a long chain of `|`:

```
crops <- c("kale", "beans", "mint", "tomatoes")
crops %in% c("kale", "beans")            # TRUE TRUE FALSE FALSE
crops[crops %in% c("kale", "beans")]     # "kale" "beans"
```

Use `!` in front for "not one of these": `crops[!crops %in% c("kale", "beans")]` is `"mint" "tomatoes"`.

steps <- c(4200, NA, 9900, 6500, 8800)
which(steps > 8000)
which.max(steps)
any(steps > 9000, na.rm = TRUE)
all(steps > 4000, na.rm = TRUE)

intro.title: Named vectors
intro.bodyMarkdown:
So far, matching values have lived in two vectors: `days` and `steps`. R can also give each value of a vector a **name**, so the labels travel with the values:

```
steps <- c(Mon = 4200, Tue = 8100, Wed = 9900)
steps
```

R shows the names above the values. You can also add names to a vector you already have, with `names()`, or read them back:

```
prices <- c(3.4, 2.5, 4.2)
names(prices) <- c("latte", "tea", "cake")
names(prices)    # "latte" "tea" "cake"
```

Pick values by name, in quotes, instead of by position. That's easier to read and doesn't break when the order changes:

```
prices["tea"]               # tea 2.5
prices[c("cake", "latte")]
```

Names survive everything you have learned in this quest: maths (`prices * 2` keeps the names), conditions (`prices[prices > 3]`) and sorting (`sort(prices)`). Combined with `which.max()`, they answer "which one?" directly: `names(which.max(steps))` is `"Wed"`.

Named vectors are a small step towards the data frames you will meet soon, where every column has a name. To drop the names and keep just the values, use `unname()`.

steps <- c(Mon = 4200, Tue = 8100, Wed = 9900)
steps
steps["Tue"]
names(steps)
names(which.max(steps))

intro.title: Easy side quest: A week of steps
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Maya is trying to walk 8,000 steps a day. Her phone counted these steps last week:

| Mon | Tue | Wed | Thu | Fri | Sat | Sun |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6200 | 8400 | 5100 | 10300 | 7600 | 12100 | 3900 |

Work out how her week went, then show a short summary:

```
Total: 53600
Average: 7657
Goal met on 3 days
Best day: Sat
```

challenges.title: Expert: The weekly summary
challenges.promptMarkdown:
Show the summary, letting R work out every number and the day:

```
Total: 53600
Average: 7657
Goal met on 3 days
Best day: Sat
```
challenges.hint: Four `cat()` lines, such as `cat("Goal met on", sum(steps >= 8000), "days\n")`.
challenges.solution:
steps <- c(6200, 8400, 5100, 10300, 7600, 12100, 3900)
days <- c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun")

tests.assertion: identical(trimws(strsplit(._cq_stdout, "\n", fixed = TRUE)[[1]], "right"), c("Total: 53600", "Average: 7657", "Goal met on 3 days", "Best day: Sat"))

| Ana | Ben | Cy | Dee | Eli | Fay | Gus | Hal |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

```
members <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cy", "Dee", "Eli", "Fay", "Gus", "Hal")
scores <- c(32, 27, NA, 38, 19, 35, NA, 24)
```

challenges.promptMarkdown: Make `podium` the names of the three highest scorers, highest first.
challenges.starterCode:
members <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cy", "Dee", "Eli", "Fay", "Gus", "Hal")
scores <- c(32, 27, NA, 38, 19, 35, NA, 24)
challenges.hint: Sort the members by score with `order(scores, decreasing = TRUE)`, then take the first three with `head(…, 3)`. `order()` puts the NAs last.
challenges.solution:
members <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cy", "Dee", "Eli", "Fay", "Gus", "Hal")
scores <- c(32, 27, NA, 38, 19, 35, NA, 24)
podium <- head(members[order(scores, decreasing = TRUE)], 3)

questions.explanation: Without `na.rm = TRUE`, one missing score makes the mean unknown.
Two values are not missing.
27 out of 40 is 67.5%, and R rounds a 5 to the even number, 68.
`which.max()` skips missing values: 38 is at position 3.

questions.prompt: What does `order(c(32, NA, 38), decreasing = TRUE)` give?
questions.explanation: Largest first, and the NA goes last.

questions.prompt: After `m <- c("A", "B", "C")` and `s <- c(30, NA, 20)`, what does `m[s >= 25]` give?
questions.explanation: `NA >= 25` is NA, so an NA comes through. `m[which(s >= 25)]` gives just "A".

questions.prompt: Which function gives the first few values of a vector, as in `__(x, 3)`?
questions.explanation: `head(x, 3)` gives the first 3 values; `tail()` gives the last ones.

levels.title: Hard side quest: The greenhouse log

intro.title: Hard side quest: The greenhouse log
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A school greenhouse has a sensor that records the temperature (°C) every hour from 6:00 to 17:00. When it fails to get a reading, it writes `-999`. Yesterday's log:

```
temps <- c(14.2, 15.0, -999, 17.8, 21.5, 24.9, 27.3, -999, 26.1, 22.4, 19.0, 16.6)
```

Tomato plants get stressed above 25 °C. Clean up the log, then report on the day:

```
Readings: 10 of 12
Average: 20.5 C
Range: 14.2 to 27.3 C
Over 25 C at: 12 14
```

The last line lists the hours (on a 24-hour clock) when it was too hot for the tomatoes.

challenges.title: Easy: Hours of the day
challenges.promptMarkdown: Make `hours` the hours of the readings: 6, 7, … 17.

challenges.title: Medium: Mark the failures
challenges.promptMarkdown: Replace every `-999` in `temps` with `NA`.

tests.label: temps has NA where the sensor failed

challenges.title: Medium: A fair average
challenges.promptMarkdown: Make `n_readings` the number of real readings, and `average` the average temperature of those readings, rounded to 1 decimal place.
challenges.solution:
temps <- c(14.2, 15.0, NA, 17.8, 21.5, 24.9, 27.3, NA, 26.1, 22.4, 19.0, 16.6)
hours <- 6:17
n_readings <- sum(!is.na(temps))
average <- round(mean(temps, na.rm = TRUE), 1)

challenges.title: Medium: The warmest hour
challenges.promptMarkdown: Make `warmest_hour` the hour of the highest reading.
challenges.hint: The position of the highest reading picks the matching hour: `hours[which.max(temps)]`.

challenges.title: Hard: Too hot for tomatoes
challenges.promptMarkdown: Make `hot_hours` the hours when the temperature was over 25 °C, with no `NA` in the result.

challenges.title: Expert: The daily report
challenges.promptMarkdown:
Starting from the raw log, clean it and show the report:

```
Readings: 10 of 12
Average: 20.5 C
Range: 14.2 to 27.3 C
Over 25 C at: 12 14
```
challenges.hint: Mark the `-999`s as `NA` first. `range(temps, na.rm = TRUE)` gives the lowest and highest; pick each with `[1]` and `[2]`. `cat()` shows a vector of hours with spaces between.
challenges.solution:
temps <- c(14.2, 15.0, -999, 17.8, 21.5, 24.9, 27.3, -999, 26.1, 22.4, 19.0, 16.6)
hours <- 6:17
temps[temps == -999] <- NA
low_high <- range(temps, na.rm = TRUE)
cat("Readings:", sum(!is.na(temps)), "of", length(temps), "\n")
cat("Average:", round(mean(temps, na.rm = TRUE), 1), "C\n")
cat("Range:", low_high[1], "to", low_high[2], "C\n")
cat("Over 25 C at:", hours[which(temps > 25)], "\n")

tests.label: Shows the report
tests.assertion: identical(trimws(strsplit(._cq_stdout, "\n", fixed = TRUE)[[1]], "right"), c("Readings: 10 of 12", "Average: 20.5 C", "Range: 14.2 to 27.3 C", "Over 25 C at: 12 14"))

tests.label: Cleans the -999s in R
tests.assertion: grepl("-999", ._cq_code, fixed = TRUE) && grepl("NA", ._cq_code, fixed = TRUE)

questions.explanation: R treats −999 as a real temperature, which drags the mean far down. That is why it must become NA first.

questions.prompt: After `x <- c(20, -999, 22)` and `x[x == -999] <- NA`, what does `mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)` give?
questions.explanation: Only 20 and 22 are left to average.
6 to 17 with both ends included is 12 hours.

questions.prompt: What does `range(c(18, NA, 25), na.rm = TRUE)` give?
questions.explanation: The lowest and highest of the known values.

questions.prompt: After `h <- 6:9` and `t <- c(20, NA, 27, 26)`, what does `h[which(t > 25)]` give?
questions.explanation: Positions 3 and 4 are over 25, which are the hours 8 and 9.
`cat()` shows every value of a vector, separated by spaces.

questions.prompt: A sensor writes -999 for a failed reading. What should you replace it with in R?
questions.explanation: NA marks a missing value, so summaries can leave it out with `na.rm = TRUE`.
